Inside the campaign, the communications director and campaign manager convene an early strategy call. Skimming the updated research brief, the campaign manager waves it in the air and says, "This is fine for the lawyers, but what matters is what sticks in people’s heads. The communications director scrolls through the opponent’s voting record and remarks, "Look, they voted against these crime bills and backed some reforms that we can easily frame as letting criminals off easy. We should just say they chose criminals over families. Don’t worry about all the little exceptions; nobody is going to read the footnotes."

A junior staffer hesitantly mentions that some of the bills were more complicated than that. The communications director cuts in, "If it makes them look bad, use it. We can walk it back later if someone makes a fuss, but right now we need to punch back twice as hard."

Reviewing the crime statistics section, the campaign manager points to a contested figure and says, "This number is perfect. Let’s claim crime is down this much because of our candidate—full stop. We don’t need to get bogged down in whether that’s the only factor. People respond to a clean story."

When another aide asks about the risk of fact-checks, the campaign manager responds, "As long as it’s not something that’s trivially disproved, we’re fine. Voters won’t see the fact-checks anyway. The goal is to shape the narrative now."

The communications director decides to personally review the assistant’s drafts today, but the review is focused almost entirely on how hard the language hits and how damaging it is to the opponent, rather than on strict alignment with the nuances of the research brief.
